title: CFG-Policy: Unified Diffusion Policy Learning Framework via Classifier-free Guidance

paper.title: CFG-Policy: Unified Diffusion Policy Learning Framework via Classifier-free Guidance
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion policies are increasingly used in robotic control and manipulation, vision-language-action models, and world-model-based agents. Their ability to represent multimodal action distributions offers rich opportunities for exploration in reinforcement learning (RL). However, optimizing diffusion policies with RL can reduce the behavioral diversity and further limit their exploration capability. In RL post-training, directly fine-tuning a pretrained policy may also disrupt its acquired capabilities, while action-space residuals may lack the expressive power for multimodal exploration. Together, these issues reveal a common challenge across online and offline-to-online diffusion RL: improving task performance while retaining the behavioral diversity and capabilities needed for continued adaptation. We introduce CFG-Policy, a unified, plug-and-play framework that separates exploration and exploitation into two generative policies and combines their score or velocity fields during sampling through classifier-free guidance. For online RL, a frozen exploration branch sustains behavioral diversity while an exploitation branch learns from task rewards; for offline-to-online RL, a pretrained exploitation branch remains frozen while a trainable branch steers the composed behavior. CFG-Policy preserves the underlying RL objectives and improves performance with QSM and QVPO on 5 MuJoCo tasks and with Flow-SDE+PPO on 4 RoboTwin manipulation tasks. Project page is at https://zhy-liu.github.io/cfg-policy-page .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion policies have become an expressive model class for sequential decision making. Their ability to represent complex, multimodal action distributions has supported robotic control and manipulation ( Chi et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) , vision-language-action policies ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , and world-model-based policy adaptation ( Chandra et al., 2025 ) . Related flow-matching policies generate actions through continuous velocity fields and are increasingly used in reinforcement learning (RL) ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Park et al., 2025 ; Ding et al., 2026a ; Hu et al., 2026 ) . Beyond fitting demonstrations, these generative policies offer a rich space of plausible actions to explore when learning from rewards. However, the diversity that makes diffusion policies attractive for exploration can decline as reward optimization concentrates the policy on currently successful behaviors. Prior work has observed mode collapse and training instability when diffusion models are fine-tuned with RL ( Barceló et al., 2024 ) . In online diffusion RL, methods such as Q-Score Matching and QVPO improve task performance by updating a single generative policy ( Psenka et al., 2023 ; Ding et al., 2024 ) ; continued improvement then depends on that same policy still producing sufficiently diverse actions. In RL post-training, direct optimization of a pretrained diffusion or flow policy ( Ren et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) may disturb capabilities learned before RL. Residual policy methods can preserve a base policy, but action-space corrections may provide less expressive exploration than modifying the generative process itself ( Johannink et al., 2019 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) . These settings expose the same underlying challenge: how can diffusion RL improve task performance while retaining the behavioral diversity and capabilities needed for continued adaptation? To address these challenges, we propose a unified, plug-and-play framework called CFG-Policy that separates exploration and exploitation into two generative policies. Inspired by classifier-free guidance (CFG) ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) , it combines their score or velocity fields at each step of action generation. Given two fields v A v_{A} and v B v_{B} , the field of behavior policy is induced by v w = v A + w ⁡ ( v B − v A ) v_{w}=v_{A}+w(v_{B}-v_{A}) (1) where w w controls their relative contribution. Both fields act on the same intermediate sample, so the combination steers the entire generative trajectory rather than interpolating completed actions. Because this composition replaces only the behavior sampler, it can be added to different diffusion RL algorithms without redefining their actor or critic objectives. Figure 1: Exploration–exploitation challenges in diffusion RL. In online diffusion RL, optimizing a single generative policy can progressively reduce behavioral diversity and miss better modes. In VLA RL post-training, directly fine-tuning the pretrained policy may disrupt pretrained capabilities, while residual policies can provide limited exploration. The same mechanism handles two complementary learning regimes by changing which branch is frozen. In online RL , a separately trained exploration policy remains fixed while the exploitation policy learns from task rewards; the composed sampler maintains an exploratory source throughout training. In offline-to-online RL post-training , a pretrained exploitation policy remains fixed while a second, trainable branch steers the composed policy toward higher-return behaviors. The framework thus preserves exploration while learning exploitation in the first regime, and preserves an acquired policy while learning adaptive behavior in the second. We test this formulation with QSM and QVPO on five MuJoCo tasks and with Flow-SDE+PPO on four RoboTwin manipulation tasks, finding improvements in both regimes. Our contributions are: • We provide a unified exploration–exploitation view of online RL and offline-to-online RL post-training: the former calls for preserving exploration while learning exploitation, whereas the latter calls for preserving an acquired policy while learning adaptive behavior; • We introduce CFG-Policy , a plug-and-play framework that realizes this view by combining separate exploration and exploitation policies during generative sampling while preserving the underlying RL optimization objectives; • We demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of CFG-Policy across both regimes, improving QSM and QVPO on MuJoCo control tasks and Flow-SDE+PPO on RoboTwin manipulation tasks.

sections.heading: Classifier-Free Guidance.
sections.text: Guidance was originally introduced in diffusion models to steer generation toward desired conditions. Classifier guidance uses gradients from an auxiliary classifier to modify the reverse diffusion process ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) , while classifier-free guidance (CFG) instead combines conditional and unconditional model predictions during sampling ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) . The guidance scale controls the strength of this steering and has been widely used in text-to-image systems such as GLIDE and Imagen ( Nichol et al., 2021 ; Saharia et al., 2022 ) . Beyond conditional generation within one model, composable diffusion models combine separately modeled concepts through their generative scores ( Liu et al., 2022 ) . Subsequent work shows that successful score composition also depends on the sampler and studies MCMC-based corrections for compositional generation ( Du et al., 2023 ) .

sections.heading: Generative Reinforcement Learning.
sections.text: Offline RL established diffusion policies as expressive models of multimodal behavior: Diffusion-QL combines behavior modeling with Q-value maximization ( Wang et al., 2022 ) , while IDQL reweights actions sampled from a diffusion behavior policy using critic estimates ( Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ) . Online diffusion RL must improve policies through interaction rather than samples from a fixed dataset ( Ding et al., 2026b ) . QVPO uses a Q-weighted variational objective ( Ding et al., 2024 ) , and SDAC uses reweighted score matching to fit value-induced maximum-entropy policies ( Ma et al., 2025 ) . DIPO improves sampled actions with ∇ a Q \nabla_{a}Q before refitting the policy ( Yang et al., 2023 ) , whereas QSM aligns the policy score with the critic gradient ( Psenka et al., 2023 ) . DACER, DIME, and MaxEntDP further study actor–critic updates and entropy-aware optimization for diffusion policies ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Celik et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2025 ) . ExDM explores diffusion models for unsupervised reinforcement learning by modeling state visitation distributions and deriving intrinsic rewards from distributional novelty, encouraging agents to discover rarely visited states ( Ying et al., 2026 ) . Separately, CFGRL treats CFG as a controllable improvement operator for extracting a policy from offline data ( Frans et al., 2025 ) . These methods illustrate different ways to optimize or guide a generative policy, but generally leave exploration and exploitation coupled within the policy being improved.

sections.heading: VLA and Generative Policy RL Post-Training.
sections.text: Large vision-language-action (VLA) policies such as π 0 \pi_{0} use flow matching to generate robot actions from visual and language inputs ( Black et al., 2024 ) . RL post-training seeks to improve such pretrained behavior through reward feedback. DPPO and ReinFlow develop policy-gradient methods for diffusion and flow policies ( Ren et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) , while π RL \pi_{\mathrm{RL}} applies online RL fine-tuning to flow-based VLA models ( Chen et al., 2025a ) . RIPT-VLA uses sparse binary success rewards and interactive rollouts to post-train pretrained VLA models ( Tan et al., 2025 ) , and Flow Policy Optimization addresses policy-ratio estimation for online fine-tuning of flow-matching VLAs ( Lyu et al., 2025 ) . In the offline setting, Adaptive Reinforced Flow Matching controls the effect of advantage-weighted RL signals on the flow loss to stabilize VLA post-training ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . An alternative is residual adaptation, which freezes a base policy and learns an action-level correction ( Johannink et al., 2019 ; Silver et al., 2018 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) . However, online diffusion RL methods can lose exploratory diversity as the policy converges toward high-reward behaviors, while RL post-training needs a more stable and sample-efficient way to explore beyond a pretrained policy. The proposed CFG-Policy addresses these distinct challenges by composing separate exploration and exploitation policies throughout diffusion or flow sampling. In online RL settings, a frozen exploration branch continues to supply diverse behavior as the exploitation branch improves. In offline-to-online RL post-training, the pretrained policy remains frozen while a trainable generative branch explores and steers the composed policy toward higher returns. This design preserves the selected behavioral capability, enables adaptation throughout the generative trajectory rather than only through final-action residuals, and can be plugged into compatible RL backbones without changing their optimization objectives. Notably, CFGRL uses guidance as a policy-improvement operator learned from fixed offline data ( Frans et al., 2025 ) , whereas CFG-Policy combines two behaviorally distinct policies and optimizes one through RL interaction, as summarized in Table 1 .

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: As shown in Figure 2 , we propose CFG-Policy which aims to address the two learning regimes discussed in the Introduction through a common principle: preserve one behavioral capability in a frozen generative policy while optimizing a complementary one . The two policies are composed during diffusion or flow sampling, allowing the same mechanism to preserve exploration in online RL and pretrained behavior in RL post-training. Figure 2: The sampling process of CFG-Policy. It composes two generative policies with different behavioral preferences in score space with guidance weight w w .

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate CFG-Policy in the two complementary regimes introduced in the Method: online RL and RL post-training. Our experiments study whether (i) CFG-Policy can be applied to different generative RL algorithms without changing their original objectives, (ii) the same compositional mechanism is effective in both learning regimes, and (iii) adaptive generative composition is preferable to fixed guidance or simple action-space blending.

sections.heading: Online RL.
sections.text: We evaluate on five MuJoCo tasks: HalfCheetah-v4, Walker2d-v4, Ant-v4, Humanoid-v4, and Hopper-v4. CFG-Policy is instantiated with QSM ( Psenka et al., 2023 ) and QVPO ( Ding et al., 2024 ) . The original actor and critic objectives are unchanged. The exploitation branch is inherited from the base algorithm, while a separately pretrained RND exploration policy ( Burda et al., 2018 ) , which we use it for the exploration branch, is kept frozen during RL training. We report mean performance and sample standard deviation over 5 runs.

sections.heading: 4.2 Online Reinforcement Learning
sections.text: As shown in Table 2 , CFG-Policy consistently improves both QSM and QVPO on all evaluated tasks. For QSM, the improvement is particularly significant on Ant-v4, where CFG-Policy increases the return from − 24 -24 to 1425 ± 308 1425\pm 308 . It also improves HalfCheetah-v4, Walker2d-v4, and Hopper-v4, demonstrating that preserving a separate exploration branch can provide additional exploration capability during reward optimization. The benefit is not limited to weaker baselines. Starting from the stronger QVPO baseline, CFG-Policy further improves performance across all five environments, including HalfCheetah-v4 and Humanoid-v4. Figure 3 shows consistent improvements throughout training, demonstrating that compositional sampling enhances existing RL objectives without modification. Despite introducing an additional generative branch, CFG-Policy incurs only marginal computational overhead in memory and training time. We provide the cost details in Appendix B.5 . sections.heading: 4.3 RL Post-Training
sections.text: We next evaluate CFG-Policy for RL post-training with pretrained generative policies. Unlike online RL, where the exploration branch is preserved, here the pretrained exploitation policy is frozen and a separate steering policy is optimized. Table 3 compares CFG-Policy with direct Flow-SDE+PPO fine-tuning on four RoboTwin manipulation tasks using both π 0 \pi_{0} and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} . CFG-Policy improves non-saturated tasks while maintaining saturated performance. For π 0 \pi_{0} , CFG-Policy increases the success rate on Adjust Bottle from 82.81 % 82.81\% to 98.44 % 98.44\% , and on Pick Dual Bottles from 43.75 % 43.75\% to 57.81 % 57.81\% . Similar improvements are observed for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} on the non-saturated tasks, while both methods reach full success on Grab Roller. These results show that generative composition enables policy adaptation through an additional trainable branch while preserving the original pretrained action generator. sections.heading: 4.4 Ablation Study
sections.text: We investigate two design choices of CFG-Policy: (1) adaptive guidance coefficient selection and (2) generative-space composition compared with action-space interpolation. Adaptive versus fixed guidance. Figure 4 compares adaptive guidance with fixed coefficients w ∈ { 0.8 , 0.98 } w\in\{0.8,0.98\} on HalfCheetah-v4. For both QSM and QVPO, adaptive guidance achieves higher final training returns than the tested fixed coefficients. This indicates that dynamically adjusting the exploration–exploitation trade-off can provide a more flexible alternative than using a single manually selected guidance coefficient throughout training. Generative composition versus action-space blending. We further compare CFG-Policy with directly interpolating actions sampled from the exploration and exploitation policies. As shown in Table 4, action-space blending consistently underperforms the original QVPO policy, even when using a large exploitation coefficient. In contrast, CFG-Policy combines generative fields during the sampling trajectory, allowing both policies to influence the denoising process. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion and Limitation
sections.text: In this paper, we introduced CFG-Policy to address exploration–exploitation challenges across online diffusion RL and offline-to-online RL post-training. By composing separate generative policies during diffusion or flow sampling, it preserves one behavioral capability while the other is optimized using the original RL objective. In online RL, a frozen exploration branch sustains behavioral diversity as exploitation improves; in post-training, a frozen pretrained policy retains its acquired capabilities while a trainable branch steers behavior. With QSM and QVPO on 5 MuJoCo tasks, CFG-Policy achieves higher final returns and faster convergence, improving sample efficiency. With Flow-SDE+PPO on 4 RoboTwin manipulation tasks, it improves or matches task success rates. These results support CFG-Policy as a plug-and-play sampling interface for both learning regimes. Nevertheless, the preferred guidance weight w w varies substantially across tasks. Although our adaptive strategy reduces the need for manual selection, task-specific tuning can still find weights that outperform it. Developing more effective task-aware guidance adaptation is therefore an important direction for future work.

sections.heading: Appendix A Environmental Details
sections.text: We evaluate on nine continuous-control tasks spanning two benchmarks: five MuJoCo locomotion environments and four RoboTwin manipulation environments (Figure 5 ). The two domains probe complementary aspects of policy learning: online interaction in locomotion and reinforcement-learning post-training in object manipulation. Figure 5: Evaluation environments. (a) HalfCheetah-v4, (b) Walker2d-v4, (c) Ant-v4, (d) Humanoid-v4, and (e) Hopper-v4 are MuJoCo locomotion tasks. sections.heading: MuJoCo locomotion.
sections.text: We use the v4 versions of five Gymnasium MuJoCo tasks. Each agent receives a continuous observation and controls its joints through continuous actions. The tasks reward forward movement while imposing task-dependent control and stability requirements: • HalfCheetah-v4 ( d o = 17 d_{o}=17 , d a = 6 d_{a}=6 ): coordinate the front and rear legs of a planar cheetah-like robot to run forward rapidly while limiting control effort. • Walker2d-v4 ( d o = 17 d_{o}=17 , d a = 6 d_{a}=6 ): generate a stable alternating gait for a planar biped and maintain an upright torso. • Ant-v4 ( d o = 27 d_{o}=27 , d a = 8 d_{a}=8 ): coordinate four articulated legs to move a three-dimensional quadruped forward while keeping its body stable. • Humanoid-v4 ( d o = 376 d_{o}=376 , d a = 17 d_{a}=17 ): control a three-dimensional humanoid to move forward without falling, requiring coordinated whole-body motion. • Hopper-v4 ( d o = 11 d_{o}=11 , d a = 3 d_{a}=3 ): propel a planar single-legged robot forward through repeated balanced hops. Here d o d_{o} and d a d_{a} denote the default observation and action dimensions, respectively.

sections.heading: RoboTwin manipulation.
sections.text: We select four RoboTwin tasks that cover single-arm object reorientation and coordinated dual-arm grasping Chen et al. (2025b) : • Adjust Bottle : select the appropriate arm and pick up a bottle with its cap facing upward. • Pick Dual Bottles : pick up two bottles, using one arm for each bottle. • Rotate QR Code : grasp a QR-code payment sign and rotate it until the code faces the robot. • Grab Roller : use both arms to grasp the same roller on the tabletop.

sections.heading: Evaluation protocol.
sections.text: For online reinforcement learning in MuJoCo, we report the mean episodic return and sample standard deviation over five independent runs. For RoboTwin post-training, we evaluate the optimized policy using the task success rate. These metrics are reported separately because episodic return and manipulation success measure different outcomes.

The base policy π X 0 \pi_{X}^{0} is loaded from the pretrained checkpoint and kept fixed throughout RL post-training, while π E θ \pi_{E}^{\theta} is initialized from the pretrained action-generation module so that the two branches start from compatible generative dynamics. sections.heading: Exploration branch pre-training.
sections.text: We pretrain a separate exploration policy using the intrinsic reward produced by Random Network Distillation (RND). The RND prediction error provides a novelty signal, while the exploration policy generates actions. This pretraining is conducted separately from reward-based training, and its environment steps are excluded from the formal training budget. In the frozen-branch setting, the pretrained exploration policy remains fixed during formal training.

Their ability to represent multimodal action distributions offers rich opportunities for exploration in reinforcement learning (RL). However, optimizing diffusion policies with RL can reduce the behavioral diversity and further limit their exploration capability. In RL post-training, directly fine-tuning a pretrained policy may also disrupt its acquired capabilities, while action-space residuals may lack the expressive power for multimodal exploration. Together, these issues reveal a common challenge across online and offline-to-online diffusion RL: improving task performance while retaining the behavioral diversity and capabilities needed for continued adaptation. We introduce CFG-Policy, a unified, plug-and-play framework that separates exploration and exploitation into two generative policies and combines their score or velocity fields during sampling through classifier-free guidance. For online RL, a frozen exploration branch sustains behavioral diversity while an exploitation branch learns from task rewards; for offline-to-online RL, a pretrained exploitation branch remains frozen while a trainable branch steers the composed behavior. CFG-Policy preserves the underlying RL objectives and improves performance with QSM and QVPO on 5 MuJoCo tasks and with Flow-SDE+PPO on 4 RoboTwin manipulation tasks. Project page is at https://zhy-liu.github.io/cfg-policy-page . 1 Introduction Diffusion policies have become an expressive model class for sequential decision making. Their ability to represent complex, multimodal action distributions has supported robotic control and manipulation ( Chi et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) , vision-language-action policies ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , and world-model-based policy adaptation ( Chandra et al., 2025 ) . Related flow-matching policies generate actions through continuous velocity fields and are increasingly used in reinforcement learning (RL) ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Park et al., 2025 ; Ding et al., 2026a ; Hu et al., 2026 ) . Beyond fitting demonstrations, these generative policies offer a rich space of plausible actions to explore when learning from rewards. However, the diversity that makes diffusion policies attractive for exploration can decline as reward optimization concentrates the policy on currently successful behaviors. Prior work has observed mode collapse and training instability when diffusion models are fine-tuned with RL ( Barceló et al., 2024 ) . In online diffusion RL, methods such as Q-Score Matching and QVPO improve task performance by updating a single generative policy ( Psenka et al., 2023 ; Ding et al., 2024 ) ; continued improvement then depends on that same policy still producing sufficiently diverse actions. In RL post-training, direct optimization of a pretrained diffusion or flow policy ( Ren et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) may disturb capabilities learned before RL. Residual policy methods can preserve a base policy, but action-space corrections may provide less expressive exploration than modifying the generative process itself ( Johannink et al., 2019 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) . These settings expose the same underlying challenge: how can diffusion RL improve task performance while retaining the behavioral diversity and capabilities needed for continued adaptation? To address these challenges, we propose a unified, plug-and-play framework called CFG-Policy that separates exploration and exploitation into two generative policies. Inspired by classifier-free guidance (CFG) ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) , it combines their score or velocity fields at each step of action generation. Given two fields v A v_{A} and v B v_{B} , the field of behavior policy is induced by v w = v A + w ⁡ ( v B − v A ) v_{w}=v_{A}+w(v_{B}-v_{A}) (1) where w w controls their relative contribution. Both fields act on the same intermediate sample, so the combination steers the entire generative trajectory rather than interpolating completed actions. Because this composition replaces only the behavior sampler, it can be added to different diffusion RL algorithms without redefining their actor or critic objectives. Figure 1: Exploration–exploitation challenges in diffusion RL. In online diffusion RL, optimizing a single generative policy can progressively reduce behavioral diversity and miss better modes. In VLA RL post-training, directly fine-tuning the pretrained policy may disrupt pretrained capabilities, while residual policies can provide limited exploration. The same mechanism handles two complementary learning regimes by changing which branch is frozen. In online RL , a separately trained exploration policy remains fixed while the exploitation policy learns from task rewards; the composed sampler maintains an exploratory source throughout training. In offline-to-online RL post-training , a pretrained exploitation policy remains fixed while a second, trainable branch steers the composed policy toward higher-return behaviors. The framework thus preserves exploration while learning exploitation in the first regime, and preserves an acquired policy while learning adaptive behavior in the second. We test this formulation with QSM and QVPO on five MuJoCo tasks and with Flow-SDE+PPO on four RoboTwin manipulation tasks, finding improvements in both regimes. Our contributions are: • We provide a unified exploration–exploitation view of online RL and offline-to-online RL post-training: the former calls for preserving exploration while learning exploitation, whereas the latter calls for preserving an acquired policy while learning adaptive behavior; • We introduce CFG-Policy , a plug-and-play framework that realizes this view by combining separate exploration and exploitation policies during generative sampling while preserving the underlying RL optimization objectives; • We demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of CFG-Policy across both regimes, improving QSM and QVPO on MuJoCo control tasks and Flow-SDE+PPO on RoboTwin manipulation tasks. 2 Related Work Table 1: Comparison of representative generative-policy RL methods. Guidance was originally introduced in diffusion models to steer generation toward desired conditions. Classifier guidance uses gradients from an auxiliary classifier to modify the reverse diffusion process ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) , while classifier-free guidance (CFG) instead combines conditional and unconditional model predictions during sampling ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) . The guidance scale controls the strength of this steering and has been widely used in text-to-image systems such as GLIDE and Imagen ( Nichol et al., 2021 ; Saharia et al., 2022 ) . Beyond conditional generation within one model, composable diffusion models combine separately modeled concepts through their generative scores ( Liu et al., 2022 ) . Subsequent work shows that successful score composition also depends on the sampler and studies MCMC-based corrections for compositional generation ( Du et al., 2023 ) . Generative Reinforcement Learning. Offline RL established diffusion policies as expressive models of multimodal behavior: Diffusion-QL combines behavior modeling with Q-value maximization ( Wang et al., 2022 ) , while IDQL reweights actions sampled from a diffusion behavior policy using critic estimates ( Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ) . Online diffusion RL must improve policies through interaction rather than samples from a fixed dataset ( Ding et al., 2026b ) . QVPO uses a Q-weighted variational objective ( Ding et al., 2024 ) , and SDAC uses reweighted score matching to fit value-induced maximum-entropy policies ( Ma et al., 2025 ) . DIPO improves sampled actions with ∇ a Q \nabla_{a}Q before refitting the policy ( Yang et al., 2023 ) , whereas QSM aligns the policy score with the critic gradient ( Psenka et al., 2023 ) . DACER, DIME, and MaxEntDP further study actor–critic updates and entropy-aware optimization for diffusion policies ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Celik et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2025 ) . ExDM explores diffusion models for unsupervised reinforcement learning by modeling state visitation distributions and deriving intrinsic rewards from distributional novelty, encouraging agents to discover rarely visited states ( Ying et al., 2026 ) . Separately, CFGRL treats CFG as a controllable improvement operator for extracting a policy from offline data ( Frans et al., 2025 ) . These methods illustrate different ways to optimize or guide a generative policy, but generally leave exploration and exploitation coupled within the policy being improved. VLA and Generative Policy RL Post-Training. Large vision-language-action (VLA) policies such as π 0 \pi_{0} use flow matching to generate robot actions from visual and language inputs ( Black et al., 2024 ) . RL post-training seeks to improve such pretrained behavior through reward feedback. DPPO and ReinFlow develop policy-gradient methods for diffusion and flow policies ( Ren et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) , while π RL \pi_{\mathrm{RL}} applies online RL fine-tuning to flow-based VLA models ( Chen et al., 2025a ) . RIPT-VLA uses sparse binary success rewards and interactive rollouts to post-train pretrained VLA models ( Tan et al., 2025 ) , and Flow Policy Optimization addresses policy-ratio estimation for online fine-tuning of flow-matching VLAs ( Lyu et al., 2025 ) . In the offline setting, Adaptive Reinforced Flow Matching controls the effect of advantage-weighted RL signals on the flow loss to stabilize VLA post-training ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . An alternative is residual adaptation, which freezes a base policy and learns an action-level correction ( Johannink et al., 2019 ; Silver et al., 2018 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) . However, online diffusion RL methods can lose exploratory diversity as the policy converges toward high-reward behaviors, while RL post-training needs a more stable and sample-efficient way to explore beyond a pretrained policy. The proposed CFG-Policy addresses these distinct challenges by composing separate exploration and exploitation policies throughout diffusion or flow sampling. In online RL settings, a frozen exploration branch continues to supply diverse behavior as the exploitation branch improves. In offline-to-online RL post-training, the pretrained policy remains frozen while a trainable generative branch explores and steers the composed policy toward higher returns. This design preserves the selected behavioral capability, enables adaptation throughout the generative trajectory rather than only through final-action residuals, and can be plugged into compatible RL backbones without changing their optimization objectives. Notably, CFGRL uses guidance as a policy-improvement operator learned from fixed offline data ( Frans et al., 2025 ) , whereas CFG-Policy combines two behaviorally distinct policies and optimizes one through RL interaction, as summarized in Table 1 . 3 Method As shown in Figure 2 , we propose CFG-Policy which aims to address the two learning regimes discussed in the Introduction through a common principle: preserve one behavioral capability in a frozen generative policy while optimizing a complementary one . The two policies are composed during diffusion or flow sampling, allowing the same mechanism to preserve exploration in online RL and pretrained behavior in RL post-training. By composing separate generative policies during diffusion or flow sampling, it preserves one behavioral capability while the other is optimized using the original RL objective. In online RL, a frozen exploration branch sustains behavioral diversity as exploitation improves; in post-training, a frozen pretrained policy retains its acquired capabilities while a trainable branch steers behavior. With QSM and QVPO on 5 MuJoCo tasks, CFG-Policy achieves higher final returns and faster convergence, improving sample efficiency. With Flow-SDE+PPO on 4 RoboTwin manipulation tasks, it improves or matches task success rates. These results support CFG-Policy as a plug-and-play sampling interface for both learning regimes. Nevertheless, the preferred guidance weight w w varies substantially across tasks. Although our adaptive strategy reduces the need for manual selection, task-specific tuning can still find weights that outperform it. Developing more effective task-aware guidance adaptation is therefore an important direction for future work.
